solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Move shy baby bird (7)

blocks.note: to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy; so is to sling

annotation.surface: Someone coaxing a timid chick to get moving.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shy' reads as timid, qualifying the bird; it is really a verb meaning to throw.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: the answer is specifically a young goose, one kind of baby bird.

entries.clue: Element of impudence irks us mildly at first (7)

indicators.note: take the first letter of each of the preceding words

blocks.note: first letters of irks, us, mildly

annotation.surface: Someone's cheek gently annoying people, one small part of the rudeness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Element of' looks like 'a part of', but the Element is the chemical one, with 'of' only joining it to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Gallium is a soft metallic chemical element.

entries.clue: Small loan increases after start of expensive diets? (11)

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'expensive'
the rises come after that E

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A money headline: a small loan grows once expensive diet plans begin.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'diets' defines by example: dieting is one way a person slenderises. A 'lend' as a noun for loan is colloquial British.
annotation.definitionFit: To slenderise is to make oneself slimmer, which is what someone who diets is doing.

entries.clue: Motorway reportedly congested after current collision (6)

indicators.note: what is heard is 'packed'; it is spelt PACT
I and M come first, then the sound-alike follows

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
packed = congested; it sounds like pact

annotation.surface: A traffic report: the motorway jammed after a crash.
annotation.walkthrough: In a traffic report 'current' looks like 'recent'; it is the physics symbol I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the force of one thing striking another, as in a car crash.

entries.clue: Heavens opening in Oslo amid abnormally dense smog (8,2)

indicators.note: take the first letter of Oslo
that O goes among the other letters
the letters of 'dense smog' are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, joined by the O

annotation.surface: Someone in Oslo gasping at an unusually thick smog.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavens' sounds like the sky above the smog; it is the exclamation.
annotation.definitionFit: Both 'Heavens!' and 'Goodness me!' are mild exclamations of surprise.

entries.clue: Foreign gent kept secret goal vague (7)

indicators.note: GOAL is made vague, its letters blurred into a new order

annotation.surface: A foreign gentleman keeping quiet about his rather hazy aims.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vague' reads as describing the goal; it is what scrambles it. 'Foreign' signals a non-English word, here Spanish.
annotation.definitionFit: A hidalgo is a Spanish gentleman of the lower nobility.

entries.clue: King ate sandwiches with vigour (4)

indicators.note: HAD goes either side of R like bread round a filling

annotation.surface: A king tucking into sandwiches with gusto.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ate sandwiches' reads as a meal; 'sandwiches' is the verb that puts R inside HAD.
annotation.definitionFit: The adverb sense, as in 'push hard': an adverb for an adverbial phrase.

entries.clue: Private Eye probing today’s dire Orwellian state? (8)

indicators.note: PI pokes into the middle of the other letters
TODAY'S is in a bad way, its letters jumbled

blocks.note: PI = private investigator, a private eye

annotation.surface: The satirical magazine Private Eye investigating how bleak modern Britain has become.
annotation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine, which makes the capitals look like a title; here it is just a detective, PI.
annotation.definitionFit: Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four is the classic dystopia; the question mark marks it as an example.

entries.clue: Wreath that is left upside down (3)

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading upward turns IEL into LEI

annotation.surface: A garland abandoned the wrong way up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like 'abandoned' next to the wreath; it is only the letter L.
annotation.definitionFit: A lei is a Hawaiian flower wreath worn round the neck.

entries.clue: Element of Nabucco Verdi dramatically exaggerated (7)

indicators.note: the answer is one part of the run of letters that follows

blocks.note: the letters run from the last of Nabucco, through Verdi, into the first of dramatically

annotation.surface: A critic calling part of Verdi's opera Nabucco overblown.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dramatically' is surface colour for an opera, but it also supplies the final D.
annotation.definitionFit: To overdo something is to exaggerate it.

entries.clue: Caustic story read aloud (3)

definitions.note: 'Caustic' here is the noun, a caustic substance.

indicators.note: said out loud, LIE sounds like the answer

blocks.note: a story is a lie, a fib

annotation.surface: A cutting tale being read out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caustic' reads as a cutting remark about the story; it is the chemistry sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Lye is a caustic alkali; the noun stands in for 'caustic' used as a noun, as chemists say 'a caustic'.

entries.clue: Posturing prigs, ever so woke (11)

indicators.note: the letters strike a new pose

annotation.surface: A jibe at self-righteous prigs who are terribly woke.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Woke' looks like the past tense of wake; it is the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Woke, of social attitudes, means progressive.

entries.clue: Emperor’s head on Indian coin that’s red or blue (8)

indicators.note: the first letter of Emperor
the E is put on IND, placed after it

annotation.surface: A description of an old Indian coin bearing an emperor's head in red or blue.
annotation.walkthrough: Red and blue read as the coin's colours. Blue means smutty; red here suggests the same, as in a racy red-light sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Blue jokes and racy, red-hot material are both indecent.

entries.clue: Following male out of gloomy bar (6)

indicators.note: to be out of something is to have left it, so the male letter M departs from MORBID

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references

annotation.surface: A man stepping out of a dismal pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is the pub in the surface; it is the verb meaning prohibit.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: both mean prohibit, as in barring entry.

entries.clue: Thirteen nameless financiers drop off last of bullion (6,5)

indicators.note: N for name is removed from BANKERS
take the final letter of bullion

blocks.note: to drop off is to doze

annotation.surface: Thirteen anonymous bankers nodding off over the gold reserves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thirteen' reads as a head-count of financiers; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A baker's dozen is thirteen, from bakers adding one extra to twelve.

entries.clue: Class liable to break up around noon in particular (10)

indicators.note: 'around' means encircling, so RICKETY wraps itself about the N

blocks.note: PE = physical education, a school class

annotation.surface: A school class likely to split up at lunchtime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Break up' suggests end of term; with 'liable to' it defines RICKETY, which then wraps N.
annotation.definitionFit: Pernickety means fussy, particular about details.

entries.clue: Brandy and stuff knocked back (4)

indicators.note: something knocked back is pushed backwards, so CRAM is read in reverse

annotation.surface: Brandy and snacks downed at a gulp.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' is drinking talk beside brandy, but it reverses CRAM.
annotation.definitionFit: Marc is a brandy distilled from grape pressings.

entries.clue: Starred in role of terse kid running amok (10)

indicators.note: the letters of 'terse kid' run wild

annotation.surface: An actor who starred as a curt child out of control.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starred' is a film credit in the surface; the answer is marked with a star symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: Something asterisked is marked with an asterisk, a little star.

entries.clue: Teasing is unpleasant at home time (8)

blocks.note: an age = a period of time

annotation.surface: A complaint that being teased at home time is nasty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Home time' reads as the end of the school day; 'at home' and 'time' are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Badinage is light-hearted teasing banter.

entries.clue: Cloddish, half-cut soldiers bored by dealing with conflict (10)

indicators.note: CLODDISH is cut in half, keeping DISH
ARMY has ON drilled into it

annotation.surface: Drunken, oafish troops getting fed up with the fighting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy, which the surface uses; the wordplay takes it literally.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a lack of agreement between people is a state of conflict.

entries.clue: Law lord upset fat dunce (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, LUD is set upside down

blocks.note: 'm'lud' is how a judge is addressed in British courts

annotation.surface: A judge insulting a stout fool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Law lord upset' looks like an anagram of LAW LORD, but there is no W in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A dullard is a dunce, a slow-witted person.

entries.clue: Steal bed for infant (4)

blocks.note: the schoolroom sense: to copy someone else's work
a baby's cot, especially in American use

annotation.surface: A thief taking a baby's cot.
annotation.walkthrough: Two plain definitions sit side by side; 'for' belongs inside the second one rather than linking them.
annotation.definitionFit: Crib means both to copy illicitly and a small child's bed.

entries.clue: Mersenne ultimately enthralled by non-prime numbers too (7)

indicators.note: take the last letter of Mersenne
the E is held captive inside B-SIDES

blocks.note: B-sides: the lesser songs (numbers) on a single, not the main A-side

annotation.surface: A mathematician charmed by composite numbers as well as his famous primes.
annotation.walkthrough: Mersenne primes make 'non-prime numbers' look mathematical; the numbers are songs, and the B-side is the lesser track on a single.
annotation.definitionFit: The adverb sense, as in 'and besides, it's late': both mean in addition.

entries.clue: One putting coat on quietly afterwards (6)

annotation.surface: Someone who quietly puts their coat on after the others.
annotation.walkthrough: The coat is a layer of metal, not an overcoat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plater coats objects with a thin layer of metal.

entries.clue: Girl is more stylish without clothes (6)

indicators.note: CLASSIER is stripped of its outer letters

annotation.surface: The claim that a girl looks better undressed.
annotation.walkthrough: Stripping a word of its clothes removes its first and last letters, leaving LASSIE.
annotation.definitionFit: A lassie is a girl, in Scottish and northern English use.

entries.clue: Extremely optimistic hints about end of road blocks (8)

indicators.note: take the two extreme letters of optimistic
'about' in its sense of surrounding, so CLUES stands round the D
take the final letter of road

annotation.surface: Very upbeat tips on where the road ends up blocked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely optimistic' reads as very hopeful; it means the letters at the extremes.
annotation.definitionFit: To occlude is to block or obstruct.

entries.clue: Denied lacking heart for action (4)

indicators.note: DENIED loses its central NI

blocks.note: deletion: the central pair NI drops out of the six-letter word

annotation.surface: Someone callously refused the chance to act.
annotation.walkthrough: A six-letter word has a two-letter heart, so both middle letters go.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym, as in 'a good deed': something done.

entries.clue: Mature dons take up books for relief (11)

indicators.note: ASSUME puts on AGE like a garment

blocks.note: to assume a role = to take it up
NT = New Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: Grown-up university fellows taking up reading for comfort.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dons' are Oxbridge academics in the surface; here it is the verb meaning puts on.
annotation.definitionFit: Assuagement is the easing of pain or distress, relief.

entries.clue: The main largely aquatic mammal (3)

indicators.note: most of SEAL, losing its last letter

blocks.note: a seal is an aquatic mammal

annotation.surface: A description of the chief, mostly aquatic mammal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The main' looks like 'the chief' in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A poetic, old-fashioned sense: 'the main' is the open ocean, as in the Spanish Main.

entries.clue: Character returned from rendezvous (3)

indicators.note: the answer is inside the next word, read backwards

annotation.surface: Someone coming back from a secret meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as a person returning; it is a letter of the alphabet, spelt out as a word.
annotation.definitionFit: The British name of the last letter, and a letter is a character.

entries.clue: Stalemate is very close (4,3)

blocks.note: dead = very, as in dead easy

annotation.surface: A game of chess where the stalemate is almost upon us.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very close' reads as 'nearly there'; 'close' is the noun, an ending.
annotation.definitionFit: A dead end is a situation where no progress is possible, a stalemate.

entries.clue: Cover for privates in unknown war zones (1-6)

blocks.note: a front is where fighting happens

annotation.surface: Protection for private soldiers in an unnamed war.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Privates' in a war setting look like soldiers; they are the private parts. Y-fronts are men's briefs, British underwear.
annotation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are men's underpants, covering the privates.
